newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania to privatise arms industry - minister.
newsitem.headline: Romania to privatise arms industry - minister.

text.p: Romania's defence minister said on Thursday that the ex-communist country plans to privatise its weapons industry in a bid to bring its military structures in line with Western standards.
"The weapons industry is a sensitive issue, but solutions to put it back on track are already looming at the horizon," Victor Babiuc, a civilian, told a news conference.
Babiuc, a member of the centrist coalition which replaced leftists after last November's elections, said a blueprint for arms industry privatisation should be ready by next month.
"I have asked the army's procurement department to draft a privatisation programme for the defence industry, which should be ready by February," he said, declining to elaborate.
The state had preserved a monopoly of the defence sector after the 1989 fall of communism.

Echoing Bucharest's renewed efforts to have Romania included in a first wave of admissions into the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation as the Western defence alliance goes ahead with its eastward expansion plans, Babiuc said:
"The question is not whether Romania will join NATO, but when. Our task is to make it clear that Romania should be admitted in a first wave, and by all means alongside Hungary."
He also announced plans to seek foreign investors to modernise Romania's army -- outside Russia, the second-largest military force in eastern Europe after Poland.
"We want to find investors to upgrade our arms technologies in order to produce weapons and ammunition not only for Romania, but also for NATO member countries."
A maverick member of the defunct Moscow-led Warsaw Pact under late dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, Romania never allowed foreign troops on its soil, but built up a large arms industry of its own.

Its defence sector was badly hit by cuts in orders and funds in the post-communist era, when the country made sweeping reforms of its military, aimed at boosting its hopes of joining the Western defence umbrella.

The U.S. Bell Helicopter, a unit of Textron Inc, signed a deal last year to take over Romanian helicopter maker Intreprinderea Aeronautica Romana SA (IAR) and to start production of Cobra attack helicopters in the Balkan country.

Bell executives are expected next week at the IAR plant, based in the Transylvanian city of Brasov, to resume talks on the $1.0 billion project to co-produce 96 twin-engined AH-1W Super Cobra attack helicopters at IAR, plant officials said.
